title: Corpus-citation hygiene: verifiable sources only (H0.4)
description: Attribution hygiene per traction-roadmap H0.4: every reference to 'the corpus' (an unpublished, unverifiable game collection) is removed from attribution_source and historical_notes. Nine rows are reworded to cite only public, dated games and published works (the claims are unchanged; dated master games are verifiable in any public database). One row, the Novosibirsk 10...Bg7 line, relied on the corpus as its load-bearing source and is WITHDRAWN entirely (all three fields cleared) pending re-sourcing under the H4.4 graded-evidence policy; its own notes conceded the corpus did not support first-play. The three Maroczy Bind rows keep their byte-identical source string deliberately: the same reference genuinely supports all three claims, and the per-row context lives in historical_notes.

fields.historical_notes: Named for the Brazilian champion Octávio Trompowsky (1897–1984), who took up 2.Bg5 in the 1930s–40s; he popularised rather than invented it – 2.Bg5 appears in earlier master play (e.g. Levitzky–Burn, 1912), well before his own earliest example (Trompowsky–Endzelins, Munich Olympiad 1936). The line also carries the alternate eponyms Opočenský and Ruth; resurrected at GM level from the 1980s by Julian Hodgson.

fields.attribution_source: Named for Alekhine, who introduced the defence at Budapest 1921 (Sämisch–Alekhine and Steiner–Alekhine, both 1 Sep 1921); naming per Wikipedia 'Alekhine's Defence' citing Hooper & Whyld and the 1922 Fahrni monograph 'Die Aljechin-Verteidigung'.
fields.historical_notes: 1.e4 Nf6. Named for Alexander Alekhine, who introduced it at master level at Budapest 1921; the move itself predates him (with antecedents from the late 1880s, e.g. Blackburne, 1889), so the eponym marks the introducer, not the inventor.

6.Bg5 e6 7.f4 b5. A self-eponym via own practice and published analysis: 7...b5 appears as early as Reicher–Krogius, Ploesti 1957, and Polugaevsky's own games run from 1959 (e.g. Zagorovsky–Polugaevsky); his sustained play and analysis gave the line his name. Attribution on this child node only; the parent Najdorf head is named for Miguel Najdorf.

1.e4 c5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5. The move long predates its namesake – it appears as early as Von der Lasa's Berlin games of 1836–37 – but Nicolas Rossolimo made it a respected weapon through frequent use from 1948 (Bad Gastein), and the line took his name (Benko, 1975). A popularizer, not the inventor.

fields.attribution_source: Sveshnikov, 'The Complete Sveshnikov Sicilian' (Gambit, 2003); the position occurs as early as Tarrasch–Mieses 1888, antedating Pelikán's 1972 Buenos Aires game by 84 years.
fields.historical_notes: The position itself was reached as early as 1888 (Tarrasch–Mieses); Pelikán adopted it as Black in the 1950s–70s in Argentina; Sveshnikov's analysis from the 1970s onwards turned it into mainline theory and the line carries his name today. Hence the alias 'Lasker-Pelikán'.
The position dates back to Wemmers–Riemann, 1880, but the Berlin Wall as a modern weapon at world-championship level is owed to Kramnik's 2000 match. Almost every elite tournament since features it.

fields.attribution_source: Named for Frank Marshall, who unveiled 8...d5 against Capablanca (Capablanca–Marshall, New York 1918); pre-history per Edward Winter, 'The Marshall Gambit' (chesshistory.com).
fields.historical_notes: 8...d5 gambit in the Ruy López. Named for Frank Marshall after he sprang it on Capablanca at New York 1918 (Capablanca defended and won). The idea predates that game — the 8.c3 d5 position appears as early as Walbrodt, Havana 1893 — so the 1918 game is the famous reveal that fixed the name to Marshall, not the line's first occurrence.

Named by Tartakower at the 1929 Barcelona tournament, where the local organisers asked the masters to invent something with a 'Catalan' flavour. Today closely associated with Vladimir Kramnik and Boris Gelfand at elite level.
Rubinstein's handling of the line at the 1924 South Tyrol tournament gave it the place-name we still use a century later.
